extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, and federal courts (judges and clerks)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factual guidance for evaluating prosecution-history estoppel and application of the doctrine of equivalents (Festo framework), including the presumption of surrender from narrowing amendments and the three recognized rebuttal grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of surrender from narrowing or unexplained amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrowing amendment (including an 'unexplained' amendment) made during prosecution triggers a rebuttable presumption that the patentee surrendered the entire territory between the original and the amended limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Festo VIII, 535 U.S. at 740–41. The presumption arises when the original claim as presented covered the alleged equivalent and the claim was subsequently narrowed; it applies whether the amendment was made for patentability or left unexplained. The party seeking to rely on the doctrine of equivalents must attempt to rebut this presumption under the Court's rebuttal criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of surrendered territory — 'entire territory between original and amended limitations'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the presumption applies, the surrendered territory presumptively includes the entire intervening territory between the scope of the originally presented claim and the narrowed claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must determine 'what territory the amendments surrendered' (Festo, 535 U.S. at 741). This requires attention to what was actually claimed and disclosed during prosecution; hindsight speculation about hypothetical claim language is improper. Disputes can arise over whether the original claim in fact encompassed the accused equivalent (e.g., whether a broader literal claim could have been presented consistent with the specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal criterion — unforeseeability of the equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee can rebut the presumption by showing that the accused equivalent would have been objectively unforeseeable to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an intensely factual inquiry: the trial court should assess evidence about the state of the art, custom and usage of terms in the relevant art, the level of ordinary skill, the bounds of the prior art, and expert testimony. The appellate court remanded to allow parties to introduce evidence on unforeseeability; trial-court findings on this issue deserve deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal criterion — tangentiality of the amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee can rebut the presumption by showing that the reason for the narrowing amendment was only tangentially related to the particular equivalent in question (i.e., the amendment was peripheral to the accused equivalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee must explain how the rationale for adding or changing claim language was peripheral to the accused equivalent. Tangentiality is meant to permit courts to honor the objective intent of amendments where the surrendered subject matter bears only a peripheral relation to an alleged equivalent (example: amendment to adjust the top end of a claimed range may be tangential to equivalents beneath the range). Whether tangentiality is satisfied depends on the prosecution history and the patentee's stated rationale; courts should examine the record rather than rely on hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal criterion — 'some other reason' the patentee could not reasonably have been expected to describe the equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee can rebut the presumption by showing there was some other reason (linguistic or practical) that the patentee could not reasonably have been expected to describe the insubstantial substitute in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include shortcomings of language or other constraints that would have prevented the drafter from describing the equivalent. Arguments that an equivalent was merely 'inferior' or 'unacceptable' do not typically satisfy this criterion if the patentee could reasonably have described the equivalent (e.g., by using broader descriptive terms such as 'aluminum', 'metal', or claim phrasing like 'at least one sealing ring'). Courts should avoid using hindsight to rewrite the prosecution record; the inquiry focuses on what a careful drafter could reasonably have been expected to claim at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability principle limiting doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents does not encompass subject matter that the patent drafter could have foreseen during prosecution and thus could have included in the claims; it protects only against insubstantial and unforeseeable substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreseeability reconciles the notice function of claims with the protective function of the doctrine of equivalents and can be applied both to rebut estoppel presumptions and more broadly to bar foreseeable equivalents outside the estoppel context. Application of foreseeability requires factual assessment of the state of the art at the time of drafting and amendment, and judges should consult expert evidence to approximate what a careful drafter would have foreseen and claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (§112, ¶6) and literal scope including structural equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'sealing means' or similar means-plus-function limitation under §112, ¶6 can literally encompass structural equivalents disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the original claim used means-plus-function language, the literal scope of the original claim may have included structural equivalents; this affects whether an amendment actually narrowed coverage of an accused equivalent. Courts should analyze whether the original 'means' limitation literally encompassed the accused structure before concluding that the amendment surrendered that territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides presumption and rebuttal issues — court role and procedural posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of the presumption of surrender and whether it has been rebutted is for the court (analogous to Markman for claim construction), but many aspects involve factual findings appropriate for the trial court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appellate court emphasized that while the legal determination of whether estoppel applies is for the court, the factual elements (particularly unforeseeability) require a trial record and evidentiary presentation. Some judges warned against converting tangentialness and 'other reason' inquiries into pure questions of law without permitting trial evidence. Remand to the district court is appropriate to receive evidence and make factual findings on unforeseeability (and, where contested, on other factual matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary and remedial consequences on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If the trial court determines the patentee has failed to rebut the presumption, prosecution-history estoppel bars reliance on the doctrine of equivalents; if the patentee succeeds in rebuttal for particular equivalents, the court may reinstate findings of equivalency as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On remand parties may introduce evidence regarding unforeseeability and related factual matters; the district court should evaluate evidence and make findings. If rebuttal succeeds for particular accused equivalents, courts may reinstate prior findings (including jury findings) of equivalence in fact.
